<reason>A wins a close, high-skill debate. B landed the flashiest hits: catching A's self-serving inertia theory, flagging auto-escalation as outside the motion's text (forcing A to drop it), and twice weaponizing A's concession that opt-outs skew toward stressed lower-paid workers—never answered by A. But B left two deeper burdens untouched: the asset-shifting/regressivity indictment of deductions' efficiency (pressed in A1.3 and A2.7, never rebutted), which discounts B's entire "new dollars" mechanism, and the outright concession that "no deduction touches zero," which ceded the extensive margin. B's relocation to already-enrolled middle earners rested on a bare assertion ("overwhelmingly hold accounts"), and its elegant salience-theft answer to A's Q1 doesn't survive inspection, since responding to a deduction requires the very action that breaks a default. A's route—convert non-actors, unlock the otherwise-uncaptured employer match, compound from the twenties—survived in trimmed form, and A's closing cleanly answered B's match-strip and crystallized the comparative. B's clipped R2 (execution cost per protocol) removed its payoff at the moment of zoom-out.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's R1 double-catch—exposing that A's inertia is strong enough to hold nine in ten for decades yet weak enough for a one-phone-call opt-out, and that A reached for escalation beyond the motion—was the sharpest rebuttal of the debate. A's A4.3 salience repair ("hardship is loud while enrollment is silent") was the best single answer, but it conceded the opt-out skew that powered B's closing.</best_rebuttal>
